title: Spotify
brief: Design a music streaming service like Spotify. Millions of people search a huge catalog, press play and expect sound within a fraction of a second. Audio files are small, the catalog is big, and every play must be counted so artists get paid. This is a general design from public knowledge, not how any company builds it.

functional: Browse and search tracks, albums and artists.
Play a track, with the next one starting without a gap.
Create and edit playlists, including shared ones.
Suggest music, such as a weekly personal mix.

nonFunctional.name: Start time
nonFunctional.target: Sound starts within 300 ms of pressing play at the 99th percentile

nonFunctional.name: Continuity
nonFunctional.target: Playback never stalls on a normal connection

nonFunctional.name: Play counts
nonFunctional.target: No play lost, none counted twice in royalty reports

nonFunctional.name: Availability
nonFunctional.target: Playback works 99.95% of the time, even if search or recommendations are down

estimate.note: Every figure is an assumption you can move. Audio is small, but many people listen at once, so egress bandwidth and the play event rate set the size.

outputs.label: Egress bandwidth at peak
outputs.note: All of it leaves through CDN edges.

outputs.label: Origin bandwidth after the cache
outputs.note: Only cache misses reach blob storage.

outputs.label: One track file
outputs.note: Small, so a whole track is cheap to prefetch or download.

outputs.label: Play events per second
outputs.note: Each finished or skipped track is one event into the pipeline.

outputs.label: Play events per day
outputs.note: Assumes the peak rate held all day, so an upper bound.

api.does: Checks the plan and region, then returns signed chunk URLs on the CDN.
Returns ranked tracks, albums and artists.
Applies add, remove or move operations. A stale baseVersion is merged, not refused.
Issues an encrypted offline copy with a licence that expires unless renewed.
Reports a play. eventId lets the server drop retried duplicates.
Returns shelves, including the weekly mix prepared offline.

data.fields: trackId, albumId, artistIds, title, duration, files per bitrate
data.why: Written when labels deliver, read constantly. Cache it hard and replicate widely.

data.fields: playlistId, ownerId, version, [trackId, addedBy] x N
data.why: Small, write heavy, one document per list. Versions allow collaborative edits.
Huge write volume and never updated. The log is the source of truth for royalties.
Looked up when a device reconnects, to renew or revoke.

evolution.title: Metadata plus files
evolution.problem: Start simple: a catalog of tracks and one place to keep the audio files.
evolution.change: An API service looks up a track in the catalog store and streams the file from blob storage (cheap, durable file storage). Files are cut into small chunks of a few seconds so playback can start before the whole file arrives.

evolution.title: Put a CDN in front of audio
evolution.problem: At peak the estimator shows several Tbit/s leaving the system. Blob storage cannot serve that, and far-away users get high start times.
evolution.change: A CDN (caches near users) serves the chunks. Popular tracks are hot, so the hit ratio is high. The app only hands out signed chunk URLs, and the player prefetches the next few chunks and the next track.
evolution.numbers: origin bandwidth is egress times the miss ratio

evolution.title: Playlists as a small hot data set
evolution.problem: Playlists are tiny but written all the time, and shared ones are edited by several people at once. Last write wins would lose edits.
evolution.change: A playlist store keeps one versioned document per list. Edits are sent as operations against a version and merged on the server, so two people adding a track both succeed.

evolution.title: Search
evolution.problem: Finding a track among a huge catalog by title, artist or a typo with a database scan is slow and cannot rank.
evolution.change: A search index is built from the catalog (a copy, rebuilt as labels deliver new tracks). It handles typos and prefixes and ranks by popularity. Playback does not depend on it.

evolution.title: Count plays for royalties
evolution.problem: Artists are paid per play. Counting inside the request path is slow, and retries from flaky phones create duplicates.
evolution.change: The player sends play events with a unique eventId. They land on a partitioned log. An aggregator drops duplicates and totals plays per track in a royalty ledger. At-least-once delivery plus dedupe gives exactly-once counts.
evolution.numbers: play events per second in the estimator

evolution.title: Weekly mixes, computed offline
evolution.problem: Recommending from the full listening history cannot run when a user opens the app.
evolution.change: A batch job reads play history on a schedule, computes each person's mix ahead of time and writes it as a playlist. Opening the app is then a plain playlist read.

steps.say: The player asks the API service to play a track.
The service reads the track and checks plan and region. It returns signed chunk URLs.
The player asks the CDN for the first chunk. A popular track is already cached there.
On a miss the edge fetches the chunk from blob storage once, then keeps it.
The player buffers a few chunks ahead and prefetches the next track, so a weak network does not cause a pause.
When the track ends or is skipped, the player reports a play event with a unique id.

flows.name: Count a play, build a mix

steps.say: A play event reaches the API service, which appends it to the log without waiting for any counting.
The aggregator reads the log, skips event ids it already processed and adds up plays per track.
Totals are written to the royalty ledger. Reports later read from here.
Separately, the nightly mix builder reads the same history from the log.
It writes each person's mix as a playlist, ready for the next time they open the app.

deepDives.title: Chunk size and prefetching
deepDives.question: How big should audio chunks be, and how far ahead should the player load?

options.name: One whole file per track
options.cons: Start waits on a big download. A skip wastes the rest. Poor cache reuse across bitrates.

options.name: Small chunks of a few seconds
options.pros: Fast start. A skip wastes little. Chunks are cached and reused.
options.cons: Many more requests and URLs to sign.

options.name: Small chunks plus aggressive prefetch
options.pros: Next track starts instantly and weak signal is hidden by the buffer.
options.cons: Wasted bytes when the user skips. Costs mobile data.

deepDives.because: Start time is the headline feature. Prefetch only a short buffer on mobile data, a longer one on Wi-Fi, and always the first chunk of the likely next track.

deepDives.title: Editing a shared playlist
deepDives.question: Two people add tracks to the same playlist at the same moment. What happens?

options.name: Lock the playlist
options.cons: Offline edits and slow phones block everyone.

options.name: Versioned operations, merged on the server
options.pros: Add, remove and move are small operations that mostly commute. Offline edits replay later.
options.cons: Needs merge rules, for example for two moves of the same track.

deepDives.because: Playlists are small, so merging is cheap. The client sends its base version and operations. The server rebases them on top of newer edits.

deepDives.title: Offline downloads and licences
deepDives.question: How do we let people listen without a network yet still respect the rights holders?

options.name: Plain files on the device
options.cons: Can be copied and kept forever after cancelling.

options.name: Encrypted files plus an expiring licence
options.pros: Files are useless without a device key. The licence expires, so cancelled users lose access.
options.cons: The device must check in now and then (for example every 30 days). Key handling is hard to get right.

deepDives.because: The files are small, so downloading is cheap. The check-in renews the licence, and the server can revoke it per device. The play events recorded offline are uploaded later with their original ids.

deepDives.title: Counting plays exactly once
deepDives.question: Retries, crashes and offline uploads create duplicates. How are royalty counts kept right?

options.name: Count in the request
options.cons: Slow, and a retry counts twice.

options.name: Log, then dedupe by eventId
options.pros: At-least-once delivery is easy. A seen-set or unique key removes duplicates. Replay recomputes any total.
options.cons: Totals are a little delayed. The dedupe window needs memory.

options.name: Distributed transactions
options.cons: Slow and fragile at this event rate.

deepDives.because: The log is durable, so any bug in the aggregator is fixed by replaying. Royalties are settled monthly, so a few minutes of delay is fine. Also count only plays past a minimum time, such as 30 seconds.

failures.what: A new album drops and everyone plays it
failures.impact: A sudden hot set of chunks that no edge has cached. Misses hit blob storage together.
failures.fix: Warm edges before release time, since drops are scheduled. Collapse duplicate misses so one request fills the cache.

failures.what: The CDN has a bad region
failures.impact: Playback stalls for the users routed there.
failures.fix: Use more than one CDN or edge pool and let the client retry on another host. The buffer hides short outages.

failures.what: The event log or aggregator falls behind
failures.impact: Totals are late. Mixes use older history.
failures.fix: Nothing user-facing breaks. Scale aggregator partitions, alert on lag, and replay from the log. Never drop events.

failures.impact: No search results, a stale home screen.
failures.fix: Playback depends only on the API service, catalog and CDN. Serve cached home shelves and fall back to recent and downloaded tracks.

scaling.lever: Add edge capacity and place caches inside ISP networks. Lower the default bitrate to cut bytes.
More log partitions by trackId or userId, and batch events in the app before sending.

scaling.limit: Catalog is huge but listening is skewed
scaling.lever: Cache the popular head at the edge and let the long tail come from blob storage. A small share of tracks takes most plays.

recap.key: Audio files are small, so play needs a CDN, small chunks and a buffer. The hard parts are scale of egress, shared playlists, and counting every play once.
recap.numbers: With the defaults: about 25M listeners, 4 Tbit/s egress, 200 Gbit/s at the origin, 4 MB per track and about 120K play events per second.
moves: Chunk the audio and serve it from CDN edges
Keep playlists as versioned documents with merged operations
Count plays through a log with dedupe by event id
Compute weekly mixes offline and store them as playlists
